Prompt Engineering Tutorial

From clear instructions to production workflows: explore prompt design, retrieval, tool use, testing, and reusable libraries.

Explore the slides

Design prompts as clear specifications

The tutorial progresses from how models process prompts to techniques for building and maintaining LLM applications. Start with a defined task, supply relevant context, and make the desired output explicit. Test the result before adding more complexity.

Six components of an effective prompt
ComponentPurpose
InstructionState the task the model should perform.
ContextProvide relevant background or source material.
ConstraintsSpecify length, tone, scope, and boundaries.
ExamplesDemonstrate desired input and output patterns.
RoleDefine a useful perspective for the task.
FormatDescribe the required structure, such as a table or JSON.

Choose techniques for the task

Zero-shot prompting starts with an instruction; few-shot prompting adds demonstrations. The deck also introduces task decomposition, prompt chaining, self-consistency, reflection, tree-of-thought approaches, and ReAct-style tool workflows.

Ground answers and connect tools

RAG adds retrieved evidence to the prompt and requests source-aware answers. Tool calling connects structured model requests to application functions. Grounding instructions and output schemas support reliability, alongside validation and permission checks in the application.

Evaluate, debug, and reuse

  1. Test representative inputs and difficult edge cases.
  2. Measure accuracy, consistency, format correctness, and safety.
  3. Compare prompt versions and simplify ambiguous or overloaded instructions.
  4. Monitor failures, latency, and user feedback.
  5. Store reusable templates with documented inputs, outputs, and revision history.

The slides cover summarization, code generation, data extraction, question answering, support, and domain assistants. Their examples illustrate prompt patterns rather than guarantees of correct outputs.

Slide 2: Introduction to Prompt Engineering

Open hosted slide

Read slide text
Introduction to Prompt Engineering Prompts are the instructions given to LLMs, and prompt engineering ensures AI delivers the most accurate and effective performance. 01 02 03 Prompt Engineering is the process of designing, refining, and optimizing input prompts to guide AI models like ChatGPT or GPT-4 in producing desired outputs What is Prompt Engineering • Optimizes AI Performance: Well-crafted prompts can significantly improve the relevance and accuracy of responses. • Reduces Development Time: Simplifies task execution without extensive coding. • Enhances User Experience: Tailors AI responses to specific needs, ensuring clarity and precision. Why Prompt Engineering is Important ● Building intelligent chatbots and virtual assistants ● Automating customer support and FAQ systems ● Generating and reviewing software code efficiently ● Extracting structured data from documents (OCR → JSON) ● Enhancing enterprise search with Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) ● Powering AI agents that can use tools, APIs, and workflows ● Creating domain-specific assistants for finance, tax, legal, and healthcare ● Improving content creation, summarization, and decision support Real World Applications

Slide 3: Why Prompts Matter

Open hosted slide

Read slide text
Why Prompt What is Prompt LLM and Prompt How Prompt Used 01 02 03 04 Prompts are the instructions we give to LLMs, and the clarity and structure of those instructions directly determine the quality of the model’s output Practice of designing effective inputs to guide Large Language Models (LLMs) toward accurate, useful, and reliable outputs. As LLMs become core tools in software development, business automation, and AI assistants, the quality of the prompt directly impacts: ● Response accuracy ● Reasoning quality ● Output structure ● Safety & consistency Prompt engineering is a key skill for building: ● Chatbots and copilots ● Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) systems ● AI agents and tool-driven workflows ● Domain-specific assistants (finance, tax, healthcare, etc.) Prompt Engineering Better prompts → Better intelligence → Better applications.

Slide 4: How LLMs Interpret Prompts

Open hosted slide

Read slide text
Prediction Tokenization Sensitivity Context & Guidance Key Idea LLMs do not “understand” prompts like humans — they generate responses by predicting the next token based on context Prompts are converted into tokens, and the model processes them within a limited context window. The model’s output depends heavily on - Wording and structure of the prompt, Order of instructions, provided context, System vs user roles in the conversation . Effective prompting means giving the model - clear intent, relevant context, desired format The model responds to patterns; better prompts create better patterns How LLM Interpret Prompts LLMs follow context, not intent — prompts shape the outcome.

Slide 6: Zero-Shot vs Few-Shot Prompting

Open hosted slide

Read slide text
Zero-Shot vs Few-Shot Prompting Few-shot prompting teaches the model by demonstration Key Idea: Examples improve reliability and control. The model answers with only an instruction and no examples. Zero Shot The prompt includes example questions and answers to guide output style. Few Shot Simple, common tasks General knowledge questions When to use Zero Shot ● Domain-specific tasks ● Consistent formatting needs ● Complex reasoning or structured outputs ● When to use Few Shot

Slide 7: Prompt Patterns and Best Practices

Open hosted slide

Read slide text
Clarity Structure Decomposition Reasoning Constraints Iterations Consistency • Write prompts with specific, unambiguous instructions. • Avoid vague requests like “tell me about…” • Organize prompts with sections (task, context, output format). • Well-formatted prompts improve model focus • Break complex problems into smaller, manageable steps. • Helps the model solve multi-step tasks more reliably • •Encourage step-by-step thinking for better accuracy. •Useful for math, logic, and decision-making problems. • Define boundaries such as tone, length, or allowed sources • Reduces hallucinations and irrelevant responses •Refine prompts through testing and incremental improvements. • Prompting is an experimental design process. •Use reusable templates for reliable production outputs. • Ensures stable behavior across applications. Prompt Patterns & Best Practices Key Idea: Prompt engineering is like writing a clear specification for AI

Slide 8: Advanced Prompting Techniques

Open hosted slide

Read slide text
Advanced Prompting Techniques From answering questions to solving problems with structured intelligence. 06 05 04 03 02 01 Encourages the model to reason step by step before answering. Chain of Thought Generates multiple reasoning paths and selects the best answer. Self Consistency Combines reasoning with tool usage (search, calculator, APIs). ReAct (Reason + Act) Explores multiple solution branches instead of one linear path. Tree of Thought Breaks workflows into multiple sequential prompts. Prompt chaining Asks the model to review and correct its own output. Reflection Prompting Key Idea: Advanced prompting turns LLMs into reasoning and action-driven systems.

Slide 10: Prompting for RAG

Open hosted slide

Read slide text
01 Why RAG Matters LLMs may hallucinate or lack access to private, up-to-date information. - RAG grounds responses in trusted documents 02 Retrieval Steps Relevant chunks are fetched from a vector database or knowledge source. - Example: policy docs, tax code, internal manuals 03 Context Injection Retrieved content is added into the prompt before generation. - The model answers using provided evidence 04 Grounding Instruction Prompts should explicitly restrict the model to the retrieved context - Use only the documents below 05 Citation-Friendly Outputs Encourage responses with references to source passages. - Improves trust and auditability 06 Enterprise Applications RAG enables AI assistants for search, compliance, and domain expertise. - Finance, legal, healthcare, tax, support Prompting for RAG (Retrieval-Augmented Generation) Retrieval + Prompting = Accurate, enterprise-ready AI answers.

Slide 14: Prompt Templates

Open hosted slide

Read slide text
Benefits of Using Templates Prompt Templates: Your Blueprint for Efficiency Benefits Prompt Templates 3 • Consistency: Ensures standardized outputs across similar tasks. • Efficiency: Saves time by reusing proven structures. • Adaptability: Easily modified to fit different contexts. • Ease of Use: Simplifies prompt creation for new or repetitive tasks. Examples of Commonly Used Templates • Summarization: Summarize the following text in 100 words: [Insert text]. • Translation: Translate the following text from English to French: [Insert text]. • Email Drafting: Compose a formal email to [Recipient] about [Topic]. • Brainstorming Ideas: Generate 5 creative ideas for [Topic or Goal]. Adapting Templates for Custom Use Cases 1. Customize for Tone: Adjust wording to suit professional, casual, or creative tones. Example: • Formal: Draft a professional email explaining the benefits of solar panels. • Casual: Write a friendly email encouraging readers to try solar energy. 2. Change Output Length: Specify word counts or output style. Example: Provide a bullet-point summary of the text below in under 50 words. 3. Add Context-Specific Details: Tailor prompts for specific industries. Example: Generate a list of marketing strategies for a SaaS startup in the finance sector. Consistency Efficiency Adaptability Ease of use Prompt Templates Benefits Summarization Brainstorming ideas Translation Email Draftimg

Slide 15: Prompt Debugging Techniques

Open hosted slide

Read slide text
Prompt Debugging Techniques 4 1. Identifying Issues in Prompt Performance • Ambiguity in instructions leading to incorrect AI responses. • Overly generic prompts resulting in vague outputs. • Overly complex prompts causing AI misinterpretation. • Repeated failures in achieving the desired tone or style. 2. Troubleshooting Techniques • Simplify the Prompt: Break down large tasks into smaller, manageable steps. Example: Instead of "Summarize and analyze this text," use two separate prompts: "Summarize this text" and "Analyze this summary." • Add Context: Include specific details to guide AI behavior. Example: "Write a professional email to a manager about project progress, emphasizing achievements." • Iterate and Test: Tweak words and structure, test with different inputs, and analyze results for improvement. • Use Explicit Constraints: Add instructions on output format, word count, tone, etc. Example: "Provide a response in 50 words or less, using formal language. 3. Best Practices for Testing Prompts • A/B Testing: Compare variations of prompts to see which performs better. • Include Edge Cases: Test prompts with challenging or unexpected inputs. • Log and Review Outputs: Document AI responses to identify trends or recurring issues. • Collaborative Feedback: Share prompts with peers or teams to gather improvement suggestions.

Slide 16: Building a Prompt Library

Open hosted slide

Read slide text
Chatbots Sentiment Analysis Text Summarization Building a Prompt Library Definition and Purpose of a Prompt Library What is a Prompt Library? A structured collection of reusable prompts designed for specific AI tasks Purpose: • Saves time by providing ready-to-use prompts. • Enhances consistency and efficiency in AI applications. • Acts as a resource for training and experimentation. Steps to Build a Prompt Library: 1. Planning: • Identify common tasks your AI performs (e.g., summarization, translation, chatbot responses). • Define goals for the library (e.g., scalability, task-specific focus). 2. Organizing: • Create a clear structure for storing prompts (e.g., folders, tags, or files). • Include metadata for each prompt, such as task type, examples, and output format. 3. Categorizing: • Group prompts into categories based on functionality or application. Examples of Categories: : Personalized responses for customer service. Planning Organizing Categorizing : Prompts to extract emotions or opinions from text. : Instructions for condensing articles, reports, or papers.

Slide 17: Managing a Prompt Library

Open hosted slide

Read slide text
6 Tips for Maintaining an Efficient Library: • Categorize Prompts: Organize prompts into logical groups (e.g., tasks, domains, complexity). • Documentation: Clearly document each prompt with its purpose, expected inputs, and outputs . • Regular Updates: Review and refine prompts periodically to ensure they remain effective. Version Control for Prompts: • Track changes and revisions using tools like Git or specialized prompt management tools. • Add timestamps and notes for each update to maintain clarity. Collaboration and Sharing: • Use shared platforms like Google Drive, Notion, or GitHub to collaborate with teams. • Provide clear guidelines for contributing and editing prompts. • Implement access controls to ensure prompt integrity. Managing a Prompt Library

Frequently asked questions

What is prompt engineering?

Prompt engineering is the process of designing, testing, and refining inputs that guide a language model toward the desired output.

What should an effective prompt include?

Define the instruction, relevant context, constraints, examples where helpful, role or perspective, and expected output format.

How do zero-shot and few-shot prompting differ?

Zero-shot prompting provides instructions without demonstrations. Few-shot prompting includes example inputs and outputs to show the desired behavior or format.

How does prompting support RAG?

A RAG workflow supplies retrieved passages as context. The prompt tells the model how to use that evidence, cite sources, and handle questions the supplied material cannot answer.

What is the role of prompting in tool calling?

Prompts describe tools and intended behavior, while the application executes permitted tool requests and validates arguments and results. Structured outputs help connect model responses to application workflows.

How should prompts be tested and maintained?

Use representative inputs and edge cases, compare versions against explicit quality criteria, record failures and feedback, and version reusable templates in an organized library.
